Definitely Southern, I was born and raised in SC and it sounds like a Georgia accent to me. Specifically near Atlanta but from outside the city. People raised near the city have a southern accent but it's not as pronounced as someone from north Georgia. I guess it could be called a watered down southern accent.

It's funny how accents work. I can tell which part of SC a person was raised in by their accent. For instance someone from Greenville, Pickens or Oconee County which is only 50 miles upstate from me has a different southern accent than I do. Dialect wise they are closer to the mountain people (hillbilly) but not quite as strongly as the Appalachian accent. They originally pronounced tire as "tar", fire as "far", iron as "arn". Most have lost the hardness of those pronunciations but you can still hear it a little.

Then there's Charleston, people raised there and in the suburbs have less of a southern accent and more of a brogue. It's very similar to a Boston brogue but with southern slang mixed in. This is probably because both cities have been port cities for hundreds of years. In my opinion it comes from a mixture, or stew if you will, of many different accents from around the world as people came in from all over the globe and learned English. Then there's the Lowcountry, this is the swampy low areas nearer the coast but not on the coast. They have a strange accent that is hard to explain. I like talking to them, it's like a mix of British rice plantation owner, with a touch of Cajun and African American. Very unique.

I worked with a nuclear engineer from England years ago. His name was John Stafford and he was here on a work visa for several years. Likable fellow that had worked all over the world including the northern and western states in America. He told me once that the people around here (lower piedmont area of SC) made him feel more "at home" than anywhere else he had worked in the states. When I asked him to explain he said we talk more like people in England and we are much easier for him to understand. I don't know about that but we are more traditional here than other parts of the country, we hate change. If our great-grandparents pronounced something a particular way we still pronounce it that way. Add to that most of us here originally came from England and Ireland with a smattering of French Huguenot (which mostly stayed in their own communities). The people in the Upstate (Greenville, Oconee) were mostly Scots and German immigrants.
